sub: The Eucharistic liturgy of the Syro-Malabar Church: its meaning, its order and our part in it
sec: What the word means

“Qurbana” is the Syriac word for “offering”, from the root q-r-b, “to draw near, to offer”. In the Holy Qurbana the Church offers to the Father the one sacrifice of Christ, and Christ gives himself to us as the Bread of Life.

For the Syro-Malabar Church the Qurbana is not one devotion among others; it is the source and summit of the whole Christian life (Lumen Gentium 11). Every sacrament, every feast and every prayer leads to it and flows from it.
Its roots

The Syro-Malabar Church, heir to the faith preached by St Thomas the Apostle, celebrates in the East Syriac tradition, which it received through its ancient communion with the Church of the East. Its principal Eucharistic prayer is the Anaphora of Mar Addai and Mar Mari, one of the oldest anaphoras in the whole Church, attributed to the apostles of Edessa; the Church has also approved other ancient East Syriac anaphoras for particular days.

The restored Syro-Malabar Qurbana was approved by the Holy See in 1985 and revised later. The Synod of Bishops, with the approval of the Holy See, has laid down a uniform manner of celebration for the whole Church; obedience to the Synod and to the Holy See in liturgical matters is part of our communion.
How it unfolds

1. Preparation and beginning. The priest and ministers prepare at the altar. The celebration opens with “Glory to God in the highest” and the Lord's Prayer, with the response “Holy, holy, holy”. Psalms are prayed, and the hymn “Lakhu Mara” (“To you, O Lord”) praises Christ, the resurrection of our bodies and the saviour of our souls.

2. The Liturgy of the Word. The Trisagion is sung (“Holy God, holy Mighty One, holy Immortal One, have mercy on us”). The Scriptures are proclaimed: from the Law and the Prophets, from the Apostle, and finally the Gospel, received with lights and incense. The homily breaks open the Word. The Karozutha, a litany led by the deacon, gathers the prayers of the people.

3. The Liturgy of the Eucharist. The gifts are brought to the altar while the “Onitha d'Raze” (hymn of the mysteries) is sung; the Creed is professed; the peace is exchanged. In the Anaphora the priest prays the G'hanthas (prayers of inclination) and the Kusapas (prayers of humility); all sing the Sanctus; the priest recalls the Lord's Supper and pronounces his words; he calls down the Holy Spirit on the offering (Epiclesis). Then come the breaking of the bread and the signing of the Body with the Blood.

4. Communion and dismissal. After the Lord's Prayer and the invitation “The holy things are for the holy”, the faithful receive Holy Communion. Thanksgiving follows, and the final blessing (Huttama) sends the people out to live what they have received.
What the Church believes
The Qurbana makes present the one sacrifice of Christ on the Cross; it is not a new sacrifice (CCC 1366–1367).
Under the appearances of bread and wine Christ is truly, really and substantially present, Body and Blood, soul and divinity (CCC 1374–1376).
The Holy Spirit sanctifies the gifts and the people; East Syriac liturgy expresses this strongly in the Epiclesis (CCC 1353).
The Qurbana is celebrated in communion with the Pope, our Major Archbishop and our bishop, who are remembered in the prayers.
How to take part well

Come early, prepare in silence, and follow the movements of the liturgy: standing for the Gospel and the Anaphora, bowing, signing yourself. Answer and sing with the community; the Qurbana is the prayer of the whole people.
Keep the Eucharistic fast prescribed by the Church, receive with reverence, and remain for the thanksgiving. Bring your family; teach your children the responses and their meaning.
The sanctuary and its signs

A Syro-Malabar church is built as a picture of heaven and earth. The sanctuary (Madbaha), raised and veiled, stands for heaven; the nave (Hykala), where the people stand, stands for the world; between them lies the Qestroma, the threshold where heaven and earth meet. The veil is opened at the beginning of the celebration and closed after it: Christ has opened heaven to us.

Above the altar stands the Cross without the figure of the Crucified, often called the Mar Thoma Sliba: the Cross of the risen Lord, flowering at its ends, with the dove of the Holy Spirit. The altar faces east, towards the rising sun, the sign of Christ who will come again from the east (Matthew 24:27). The ancient East Syriac churches also had a Bema in the nave for the Liturgy of the Word.
Forms, vestments and gestures

The Syro-Malabar Qurbana has three forms: the Raza (the most solemn form, for great feasts), the solemn form, and the simple form used on most days. The Synod of Bishops has laid down a uniform mode of celebration for the whole Church: the priest faces the people during the Liturgy of the Word and the concluding rites, and faces the altar, with the people, towards the east during the Eucharistic Liturgy.

The priest wears the kuthina (white tunic), the urara (stole), the zande (cuffs), the zunara (girdle) and the phaina (the large outer vestment, like a cope). Incense, lights, bowing, kissing the altar and the sign of the Cross belong to the language of the Qurbana: they teach with the body what the words say.
Questions people ask
Why do we stand so much? Standing is the posture of the risen, of people ready to go; the East has always prayed standing, especially on Sundays.

Why the long prayers of humility (Kusapas)? Before the holy Mysteries the priest, and the whole people with him, confesses unworthiness and trust in mercy. Without humility no one can come near the altar.

Why is Communion received on the tongue? According to the norms of the Syro-Malabar Church, Holy Communion is normally received on the tongue, as a sign of reverence and of receiving a gift that we do not take for ourselves. Follow the norms of your eparchy.
How often may I receive? Catholics may receive every day; a second time on the same day only within a Qurbana in which they take part.
notes: Anyone conscious of grave sin must make a sacramental confession before receiving Holy Communion (CCC 1385).
Participation in the Holy Qurbana on Sundays and days of obligation is a grave duty (CCC 2180–2181).
Liturgical texts and the manner of celebration are determined by the Church's competent authority; no individual may change them on his own (Sacrosanctum Concilium 22; CCEO c. 657).
Disputes about the liturgy must never be carried on with disrespect to the Holy Eucharist, to the altar or to the Church's pastors.
Catholics receive Communion in Catholic celebrations, except in cases foreseen by Church law (CCC 1398–1401).
The Eucharistic fast before Holy Communion is laid down by the particular law of each Church sui iuris; follow the current norm of the Syro-Malabar Church (CCEO c. 713 §2).
refs: Lumen Gentium 11; Sacrosanctum Concilium 47–48; Orientalium Ecclesiarum 1–6

sub: How the Syro-Malabar Church walks through the whole mystery of Christ, season by season
sec: Why the Church keeps a year

Christ is the same yesterday, today and for ever (Hebrews 13:8). Yet the Church does not celebrate his mystery all at once. In the course of one year she unfolds it step by step: the promise and birth of the Saviour, his manifestation, his fasting and Passion, his Resurrection, the gift of the Spirit, the mission of the apostles, the growth of the Church and the final fulfilment at his coming (CCC 1163–1171).

The liturgical year is therefore not a calendar of reminders. Each season makes present a part of the mystery, so that the faithful may enter it, be touched by it and be changed by it. The East Syriac Fathers loved to say that the Church walks with Christ through the year as Israel walked with God through the desert: feast by feast, fast by fast, towards the promised land.
Sunday, the heart of the year

Before there were seasons there was Sunday. From the day of the Resurrection the disciples gathered on the first day of the week to break bread (Acts 20:7). Sunday is the original feast, the weekly Easter, the foundation of the whole year (CCC 2174–2177).

In the Syro-Malabar tradition each Sunday has its own name within the season (for example, the Third Sunday of Annunciation) and its own set of four readings: two from the Old Testament (the Law and the Prophets), one from the Apostle and one from the Gospel. The Sunday Qurbana gathers the parish as one family around the altar.
How the dates are fixed

Two feasts anchor the year. The Nativity of the Lord is fixed on 25 December. Easter (the Qyamta) moves: it is kept on the Sunday after the first full moon following the spring equinox, according to the rule received from the Council of Nicaea (325).

Most of the year depends on Easter. Counting back: the Great Fast begins on the Monday seven weeks before Easter; the Fast of the Ninevites (Moonnu Nombu) falls a few weeks before the Great Fast; the season of Denha (Epiphany) is longer or shorter according to how early Easter comes. Counting forward: the Ascension on the fortieth day, Pentecost on the fiftieth, and the seasons of the Apostles and of Summer follow.

The year begins on the Sunday of Annunciation that falls between 27 November and 3 December, and ends with the last Sunday of the Dedication of the Church. The Syro-Malabar Church uses two sets of lectionary readings in alternate years; the official calendar published each year by the Major Archiepiscopal Curia tells which set is used.
The seasons of the Lord's coming and manifestation

1. Annunciation-Nativity (Subara). About four weeks of preparation, with the Sundays of the announcements: to Zechariah, to Mary, the birth of John, the revelation to Joseph. The Twenty-Five Days' Fast (1–25 December) belongs here. The Nativity of the Lord is celebrated on 25 December, often with a night Qurbana and, in many parishes, the ancient rite of the fire (Thee Uzhalichu) in which the faithful pass before a fire as a sign of Christ the Light.

2. Epiphany (Denha). Denha means “dawn” or “rising”. It begins on 6 January with the Baptism of the Lord in the Jordan, where the Father, the Son and the Spirit were revealed. In Kerala the night of Denha is kept with lights and the Pindiperunnal, the feast of the plantain stems decked with lamps. The Fridays of this season commemorate in turn John the Baptist, the apostles Peter and Paul, the four evangelists, St Stephen, the Greek Fathers, the Syrian Fathers, the patron of the parish and, on the last Friday, all the faithful departed.
The Great Fast, Holy Week and Easter

3. The Great Fast (Sawma Rabba). Fifty days of prayer, fasting and almsgiving. It begins on the Monday after Pethurta Sunday (the Sunday of “looking back”, of reconciliation before the fast); in many parishes ashes are blessed that day. The Wednesday of the fourth week marks mid-Lent; the fortieth Friday (Nalpathaam Velli) marks the end of the forty days of the Lord's fast.

Holy Week begins with the Saturday of Lazarus (in Kerala homes, Kozhukatta Saturday) and Hosanna Sunday (Oshana), with the procession of palms. On Pesaha Thursday the Church celebrates the Last Supper and the washing of the feet; families break the Pesaha appam at home with milk, remembering the Passover of the Lord. Good Friday is a day of mourning, fasting and the Way of the Cross; there is no Qurbana. Holy Saturday is a day of silence at the tomb.

4. Resurrection (Qyamta). Easter is the feast of feasts. The Sunday after Easter is the New Sunday (Puthunjayar), with the Gospel of St Thomas confessing “My Lord and my God”, a Sunday dear to the St Thomas Christians. The Ascension is kept on the fortieth day.
The seasons of the Church on mission

5. Apostles (Sliha). From Pentecost, when the Spirit came upon the apostles, the Church remembers their mission to the nations. The Dukrana of St Thomas, our Father in faith, is kept on 3 July; it is also kept as the day of the Syro-Malabar Church.

6. Summer (Qaita). The season of fruit: the Church, planted by the apostles, grows and bears fruit in holiness. The Assumption of Mary (15 August) usually falls in this season; many keep the devotional fast of the first fifteen days of August.

7. Elijah-Cross (Eliya-Sliba). Elijah, taken up to heaven, was expected to return before the Day of the Lord; the Cross is the sign of the Son of Man that will appear at his coming (Matthew 24:30). The Exaltation of the Holy Cross (14 September) gives the season its centre. The Eight Days' Fast before the Nativity of Mary (1–8 September) is widely kept.
8. Moses (Muse). Moses, who led the people to the edge of the promised land, turns our eyes to the end of the journey: judgment, the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come.

9. Dedication of the Church (Qudash Edta). The last four Sundays celebrate the Church as the Bride of Christ, cleansed and adorned for the heavenly wedding. The year ends where history ends: in the Church gathered with her Lord.
Feasts, commemorations and fasts

The great feasts of the Lord are the Nativity, Denha, Easter, the Ascension and Pentecost. Other great days are the Dukrana of St Thomas (3 July), the Assumption of Mary (15 August), the Nativity of Mary (8 September), the Exaltation of the Cross (14 September) and the feasts of the saints of our own Church: St Alphonsa (28 July), St Kuriakose Elias Chavara (3 January), St Euphrasia (29 August) and St Mariam Thresia (8 June), among others.

The traditional fasts (Nombu) are the Twenty-Five Days' Fast before Christmas, the Three Days' Fast of the Ninevites, and the Great Fast. Devotional fasts kept by many are the fast of the first fifteen days of August and the Eight Days' Fast in September. Fasting in our tradition is never only a matter of food: it is joined to prayer, reconciliation and almsgiving.
Living the year at home

The liturgical year is meant to enter the home. Keep the crib and the star in Subara; light lamps at Denha; keep the Nombu as a family, choosing simpler meals and giving the savings to the poor; break the Pesaha appam on Pesaha Thursday; read the Gospel of the Sunday together on Saturday evening.

Name the season at family prayer (“This is the season of the Apostles”), pray for the intentions of the season, and let children know which saints are remembered. In this way the rhythm of the Church becomes the rhythm of the family, and the home becomes a little church.
notes: The obligation to take part in the Holy Qurbana on Sundays and days of obligation is grave; only a serious reason such as illness or the care of infants excuses (CCC 2180–2181).

The exact days of obligation and the rules of fasting and abstinence for the Syro-Malabar Church are laid down by its Synod of Bishops; follow the current particular law and the circulars of your eparchy, especially outside Kerala and abroad.
Fasting must never endanger health: the sick, pregnant and nursing mothers, the elderly and those doing heavy work should consult their pastor (cf. CCC 2043).

Customs such as Kozhukatta Saturday, the Pesaha appam, Pindiperunnal and the rite of the fire are traditions of the St Thomas Christians; they vary between regions and parishes. They are signs of faith, not substitutes for the liturgy.
On the number of seasons: some calendars count Elijah, Cross and Moses as a single season; the official Syro-Malabar calendar is the norm.
The Syro-Malabar Church has no liturgical colour code like the Roman Rite; do not judge a season by colour.
refs: Syro-Malabar Church, Liturgical Calendar (published yearly) and Thaksa of the Holy Qurbana

sub: Why we confess, how to examine our conscience, how to make a good confession, and what the Church asks of us
sec: Christ gave this sacrament

On the evening of Easter the risen Lord breathed on the apostles and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit. If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven them; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained” (John 20:22–23). Through the bishops and priests, their successors, Christ continues to forgive sins in the Church (CCC 1441–1445).

This sacrament has many names: conversion, penance, confession, forgiveness and reconciliation (CCC 1423–1424). In Kerala we usually say “Kumbasaram”. It is the sacrament of the prodigal son coming home and of the Father who runs to embrace him (Luke 15:20).
Why confess to a priest?

Only God forgives sins (Mark 2:7). But God chose to forgive through his Church: Christ gave the apostles the power to forgive and to retain, which they could not use without hearing the sins (CCC 1461–1462). The priest is not a judge who condemns but a minister of mercy who acts in the person of Christ, the Good Shepherd seeking the lost sheep (CCC 1465).

Sin is never purely private. It wounds the Body of Christ, the Church. So reconciliation with God is also reconciliation with the Church (CCC 1445, 1469). Hearing the words of absolution spoken aloud gives a certainty of forgiveness that our feelings alone cannot give.
Mortal and venial sin

Mortal sin destroys charity in the heart: it is a sin whose object is grave matter, committed with full knowledge and deliberate consent (CCC 1857). Grave matter is specified by the Ten Commandments. Mortal sin, unless repented and forgiven, separates us from God for ever (CCC 1861).

Venial sin weakens charity but does not destroy it (CCC 1862–1863). Confessing everyday faults is strongly recommended: it helps us form our conscience, fight evil tendencies, let ourselves be healed by Christ and grow in the life of the Spirit (CCC 1458).
Examining the conscience

An honest examination is the first step. Some questions, following the Commandments: Do I pray daily? Have I denied my faith or been ashamed of it? Have I used God's name carelessly or sworn falsely? Have I missed the Holy Qurbana or Mass on Sundays and days of obligation without serious reason?

Have I honoured my parents and cared for them? Have I been unjust, violent or harsh at home, at work, with servants or employees? Have I harmed life: by anger, hatred, abortion, abuse of alcohol or drugs, reckless driving? Have I sinned against chastity in thought, word or deed, alone or with others, through pornography? Have I been faithful in marriage?

Have I stolen, cheated, taken bribes, failed to pay just wages or debts, wasted money while others are in need? Have I lied, gossiped, ruined another's good name, posted harmful things on social media? Have I been envious, greedy, proud, lazy in my duties? Have I neglected the poor?

Children and young people can ask more simply: Did I pray? Did I obey my parents and teachers? Did I tell lies, fight, use bad words, take what is not mine, cheat in exams, waste time on the phone, hurt anyone?
The three acts of the penitent

1. Contrition: sorrow of soul and hatred for the sin committed, with the resolution not to sin again. Perfect contrition comes from love of God; imperfect contrition (attrition) comes from fear of punishment or the ugliness of sin, and is sufficient for the sacrament (CCC 1451–1453).

2. Confession: telling the priest all mortal sins of which, after careful examination, we are conscious, with their kind and number, as far as we can (CCC 1456). Speak simply and honestly; there is no need for long stories or for naming other people.

3. Satisfaction: doing the penance the priest gives, to repair the harm and restore our habits as disciples of Christ (CCC 1459–1460). Where we have harmed others, we must also make it right: return what was taken, restore a damaged reputation, ask forgiveness.
How to make a good confession
Before: pray to the Holy Spirit for light; examine your conscience; awaken sorrow by looking at the crucifix and remembering God's love.

In the confessional: make the sign of the Cross; say how long it has been since your last confession and, if helpful, your state of life (married, student, priest or religious); confess your sins; listen to the priest's counsel and accept the penance; pray an act of contrition; receive absolution with faith. In the Eastern Churches the prayer of absolution often asks God to forgive the penitent; in the Latin Church the priest says “I absolve you”. Both are true and valid forms of the same sacrament.

A traditional act of contrition: O my God, I am heartily sorry for having offended you, and I detest all my sins because of your just punishments, but most of all because they offend you, my God, who are all good and deserving of all my love. I firmly resolve, with the help of your grace, to sin no more and to avoid the near occasion of sin. Amen. (Any approved act of contrition may be used, such as the one taught in your parish catechism.)
After: thank God; do the penance soon; repair any harm done; avoid the occasions of sin; come back regularly, not only when burdened by grave sin.
What the sacrament gives

Reconciliation with God, by which grace is restored; reconciliation with the Church; remission of the eternal punishment due to mortal sin and, at least in part, of temporal punishment; peace and serenity of conscience and spiritual consolation; and an increase of strength for the Christian battle (CCC 1468–1470, 1496).

Many people find that the hardest step is the first one, the walk to the confessional. Beyond it is the joy of the Father: “this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found” (Luke 15:24).
Children, first confession and frequent confession

Children who have reached the age of discretion (around seven) are prepared for their first confession before their first Holy Communion (CCC 1457; c. 914). Parents should go with them and confess themselves; children learn most from what they see.

The saints recommend confessing regularly, for example monthly, and before the great feasts. Many parishes offer confession during the Twenty-Five Days' Fast and the Great Fast or Lent; make use of these times.
notes: Every Catholic who has reached the age of discretion must confess grave sins at least once a year (CCC 2042, 1457).

One who is conscious of mortal sin must not receive Holy Communion without first going to confession, except when there is a grave reason and no opportunity to confess; then an act of perfect contrition must be made, with the intention of confessing as soon as possible (CCC 1457, 1385).

Deliberately hiding a mortal sin in confession makes the confession invalid and adds the sin of sacrilege; the hidden sin and the sacrilege must be confessed. Forgetting a sin is not hiding it: the forgotten sin is forgiven and should be mentioned at the next confession.
The priest is bound by the absolute seal of confession: he may never reveal or use what he hears, under the most severe penalties (CCC 1467; Code of Canon Law c. 983; CCEO c. 733).
Absolution requires real contrition and the purpose of amendment; it cannot be given to one who refuses to give up a grave sin or to repair a grave injustice.

General absolution without individual confession is allowed only in grave necessity (danger of death, or very large numbers with no possibility of individual confession for a long time); grave sins must then be confessed individually as soon as possible (CCC 1483).
Some very grave sins carry penalties whose remission is reserved; if this concerns you, speak to a priest, who will explain the path of reconciliation.
refs: Code of Canon Law cc. 959–991; Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches cc. 718–736

sub: Mamodisa and Thailabhishekam: how we are born into Christ and sealed with the Spirit
sec: Christ commands it

Before his Ascension the risen Lord sent the apostles: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). On the day of Pentecost Peter told the crowd: “Repent, and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ so that your sins may be forgiven; and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:38).

Baptism is the door of the Christian life and of the other sacraments (CCC 1213). It is called the bath of new birth (Titus 3:5) and enlightenment (Hebrews 6:4): “no one can enter the kingdom of God without being born of water and Spirit” (John 3:5).
How it is celebrated in our Church

In the Syro-Malabar Church Baptism (Mamodisa) and Chrismation (Thailabhishekam, the anointing with Holy Myron) are celebrated together, as in all the Eastern Churches. The priest is the ordinary minister of both, using the Myron consecrated by the Major Archbishop or bishop.

The rite unfolds in steps: the reception of the child at the door of the church; prayers of exorcism and the renunciation of Satan; the profession of faith (the Creed); the anointing with the oil of catechumens; the blessing of the baptismal water; the Baptism itself, by immersion or by pouring water three times, with the words “N. is baptized in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (p); the anointing with Holy Myron; the clothing in the white garment and the giving of the lighted candle.

The East Syriac form of the words is passive (“is baptized”): it confesses that it is God who acts, through the hands of the priest. Children usually receive their First Holy Communion later, after preparation in the parish.
What Baptism does

Baptism forgives original sin and all personal sins, with all punishment due to sin (CCC 1263). It makes us a new creation, adopted children of God, members of Christ and temples of the Holy Spirit (CCC 1265). It joins us to the Church, the Body of Christ (CCC 1267).

It marks the soul with an indelible spiritual seal, which no sin can erase; therefore Baptism is never repeated (CCC 1272). The weakness left by original sin remains, and the struggle against sin continues; but the baptised are never alone in that struggle.
The seal of the Spirit

Baptism, Chrismation (Confirmation) and the Holy Eucharist together are the sacraments of Christian initiation (CCC 1212). Chrismation completes baptismal grace: the baptised are anointed with Holy Myron (Chrism), consecrated by the bishop, and receive the Holy Spirit as the apostles did at Pentecost, to be strong witnesses of Christ (CCC 1285, 1303).
Like Baptism, Chrismation marks the soul with an indelible character and is received only once (CCC 1304).
Parents and godparents

Children are baptised in the faith of the Church, and parents promise to raise them in that faith (CCC 1250–1253). Godparents (sponsors) must be practising Catholics who have received the sacraments of initiation, chosen to help the child live as a Christian. They are not chosen only for family honour.
Choosing a Christian name, often the name of a saint, gives the child a heavenly friend and a model (CCC 2156).
In danger of death

In an emergency anyone, even a non-baptised person, can baptise, if he or she intends to do what the Church does: pour water on the head of the person, saying, “N., I baptize you in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (CCC 1256). Inform the parish priest afterwards, so that it can be recorded and the other rites completed.

Those who die for the faith before being baptised (baptism of blood), and catechumens who die with the explicit desire for Baptism, are saved without the sacrament (CCC 1258–1259). For children who die without Baptism, the Church entrusts them to the mercy of God and hopes for their salvation (CCC 1261).
Living our Baptism

Remember the date of your Baptism and celebrate it. Renew your baptismal promises at Easter. Teach children that the font is where they were born as Christians. Visit your baptismal church when you can.
The white garment and the lighted candle given at Baptism are a call: keep the garment clean and the light burning until the Lord comes (cf. Matthew 25:1–13).
notes: Parents should ask for the Baptism of their children within the first weeks after birth and prepare for it; delay without a just reason is not right (CCC 1250; CCEO c. 686; c. 867).
Baptism must be recorded in the parish register; the baptismal certificate is needed for later sacraments, especially marriage.
A godparent must be at least sixteen years old (unless the bishop decides otherwise), confirmed, living a life of faith, and not the father or mother of the child (c. 874; CCEO c. 685).
Baptism validly given in other Christian Churches is not repeated when a person enters full communion with the Catholic Church.
In the Syro-Malabar Church Chrismation is not postponed to a later age as in the Latin Church; a Syro-Malabar child receiving Baptism and Chrismation together has received both sacraments fully.
Children of Syro-Malabar parents belong to the Syro-Malabar Church even when baptised elsewhere; register the Baptism in your own parish and Church (CCEO c. 29).
refs: Code of Canon Law cc. 849–896; Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches cc. 675–697

sub: The sacrament of Christ's healing for the seriously ill and the elderly
sec: Christ the healer

The Gospels are full of the sick who came to Jesus: the blind, the lepers, the paralysed. He healed them as a sign that the Kingdom had come, and he sent the apostles to do the same: “anointed with oil many who were sick and cured them” (Mark 6:13).

The Church continues this ministry: “Are any among you sick? They should call for the elders of the church and have them pray over them, anointing them with oil in the name of the Lord. The prayer of faith will save the sick, and the Lord will raise them up; and anyone who has committed sins will be forgiven” (James 5:14–15; CCC 1510).
Who should receive it

The Anointing of the Sick is not only for the dying. It is for any of the faithful whose health is seriously impaired by sickness or old age: before a serious operation, in a grave illness, when the elderly become very weak (CCC 1514–1515).

It may be repeated if the person recovers and falls ill again, or if the illness becomes more serious. Do not wait until the person is unconscious; call the priest while the sick person can still pray and receive Communion.
How it is celebrated in our Church

In the Syro-Malabar Church the priest, with the family gathered around, begins with prayers of repentance and, if possible, hears the sick person's confession. The Word of God is read. The oil of the sick, blessed by the bishop (or by the priest in case of need), is used to anoint the forehead and the hands, or other parts of the body, while the priest prays for healing of body and soul, for forgiveness and for strength.
Holy Communion is then given when possible. The family answers the prayers and joins in the intercessions; their faith supports the sick person.
What the sacrament gives

The special grace of the Holy Spirit gives strength, peace and courage to bear the suffering of illness or old age; it unites the sick person to the Passion of Christ, so that suffering takes on a saving meaning; it forgives sins if the sick person could not make a confession; it restores health if that is good for the salvation of the soul; and it prepares for the passage to eternal life (CCC 1520–1523).
The sick are not useless to the Church. By offering their pain with Christ they contribute to the good of the whole People of God (CCC 1522; Colossians 1:24).
Viaticum: food for the journey

For those who are about to leave this life, the Church offers, besides the Anointing, Holy Communion as Viaticum, the “food for the journey” to the Father. Christ said: “Those who eat my flesh and drink my blood have eternal life, and I will raise them up on the last day” (John 6:54; CCC 1524–1525).
Confession, Anointing and Viaticum together are the last sacraments of the Christian, the sacraments that prepare for the heavenly homeland.
How the family can help
Tell the parish priest early when someone is seriously ill. Prepare the room: a table with a clean cloth, a crucifix, a candle, a glass of water. Keep silence and pray with the sick person.
Visit the sick, pray the rosary with them, read the Gospel to them, and help them to receive the sacraments regularly. Caring for the sick is caring for Christ (Matthew 25:36).
notes: Only bishops and priests can validly give the Anointing of the Sick (CCC 1516; c. 1003; CCEO c. 739).
Those who are conscious should go to Confession before the Anointing whenever possible.
The Anointing is not given to the dead; if death is uncertain, it may be given conditionally. After death, the Church prays for the departed.
Every Catholic in danger of death is bound to receive Holy Communion as Viaticum (c. 921).
refs: Code of Canon Law cc. 998–1007; Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches cc. 737–742

sub: The sacrament of married love in the Syro-Malabar Church
sec: God's plan from the beginning

“God created humankind in his image… male and female he created them” (Genesis 1:27). “Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother and clings to his wife, and they become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). Marriage is not a human invention; it is written into creation by God himself (CCC 1603).

Jesus restored marriage to its original dignity: “what God has joined together, let no one separate” (Mark 10:9). For Christians it is a sacrament: the love of husband and wife becomes a sign of the love of Christ for his Church (Ephesians 5:25–32; CCC 1612–1617).
The marks of Christian marriage

Unity: one man and one woman, giving themselves to each other for life. Indissolubility: a valid sacramental marriage, consummated, cannot be dissolved by any human power, only by death (CCC 1640, 2382). Fidelity: an exclusive love, without betrayal in body or heart. Openness to life: children are the supreme gift of marriage, and parents are the first teachers of the faith (CCC 1652–1653).
Free consent is the heart of marriage. No one may be forced to marry; consent given under grave fear or deception can make a marriage invalid (CCC 1625–1628).
How it is celebrated in our Church

In the Eastern Churches the priest is not only a witness: he blesses the marriage in the name of Christ, and this priestly blessing is required for validity (CCEO c. 828; CCC 1623). Marriage is called the Mystery of the Crowning in the Syriac tradition.

The Syro-Malabar rite includes the questions and the exchange of consent, the blessing of the couple, and two ancient signs: the minnu (thali), a small pendant with a cross, blessed by the priest and tied by the bridegroom around the bride's neck, and the manthrakodi, the wedding cloth blessed and given by the bridegroom to the bride. Both are signs of a covenant made before God. The wedding usually takes place within the Holy Qurbana.
Preparation

Marriage is prepared long before the wedding: by a chaste friendship, by prayer and by honest conversation about faith, children, money and families. The Church asks couples to attend a marriage preparation course and to meet the parish priest in good time; the banns are announced in the parishes.
The couple should go to Confession before the wedding and receive Holy Communion, so that they begin their married life in grace (CCC 1622).
Living the sacrament

The grace of the sacrament remains every day: it gives the spouses strength to love, to forgive, to bear one another's burdens and to raise their children in the faith. A family that prays together, goes to the Holy Qurbana together and forgives each other becomes a domestic church (CCC 1656–1658).
When difficulties come, seek help early: from a priest, a trusted counsellor or a couple in the parish. Christ who was present at Cana is present in every Christian marriage.
notes: Catholics must marry according to the canonical form: before the competent priest (or bishop or delegated cleric) and two witnesses; otherwise the marriage is invalid, unless a dispensation has been given (c. 1108; CCEO c. 828).

Marriage with a baptised non-Catholic requires the permission of the competent authority; marriage with a non-baptised person requires a dispensation. The Catholic party promises to remain faithful and to do all in his or her power to have the children baptised and raised Catholic (CCC 1633–1637).

Civil divorce does not dissolve a valid sacramental marriage. Where there is serious doubt about validity, the Church's tribunal can examine the case and, if proven, declare the marriage null (CCC 1629).
Dowry and extravagant display contradict the dignity of the sacrament and burden the poor; the Church in India has repeatedly asked the faithful to avoid them.
refs: Code of Canon Law cc. 1055–1165; Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches cc. 776–866

sub: Bishops, priests and deacons in the Syro-Malabar Church
sec: The priesthood of Christ

Christ is the one High Priest, who offered himself once for all (Hebrews 7:26–27). All the baptised share in his priesthood: they offer their lives as a spiritual sacrifice (1 Peter 2:9; CCC 1546). But Christ also chose the Twelve and gave them a special share in his mission: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19); “As the Father has sent me, so I send you” (John 20:21).

Through the sacrament of Holy Orders this mission continues in the Church until the end of time. Those ordained act in the person of Christ the Head, to teach, to sanctify and to shepherd his people (CCC 1548–1551).
Three degrees
The bishop receives the fullness of the sacrament. He is a successor of the apostles, the visible sign of unity in the local Church, in communion with the Pope and the other bishops (CCC 1555–1561).

The priest is a co-worker of the bishop: he celebrates the Eucharist, forgives sins, anoints the sick, preaches the Word and cares for the people entrusted to him (CCC 1562–1568). The deacon is ordained for service: he proclaims the Gospel, assists at the altar, baptises, blesses marriages where permitted, leads funerals and serves the poor (CCC 1569–1571).
The essential rite

In every rite the essential sign is the laying on of hands by the bishop, with the consecratory prayer asking God to pour out the Holy Spirit for the ministry (CCC 1573). Like Baptism and Chrismation, Holy Orders marks the soul with an indelible character; it cannot be repeated or taken away (CCC 1581–1583).

Only a baptised man can validly receive sacred ordination; the Church holds herself bound by the choice made by the Lord himself (CCC 1577). No one has a right to ordination; it is a call from God, discerned and confirmed by the Church (CCC 1578).
The orders in our Church

The East Syriac tradition keeps, besides the three degrees of the sacrament, the minor ministries through which candidates pass: the reader (Karoya) and the subdeacon (Hewpadiaqna). Then come the deacon (Mshamshana), the priest (Kasisa or Kasheesha) and the bishop (Episcopa). The Syro-Malabar Church is governed by its Major Archbishop and Synod of Bishops, in communion with the Pope.

At priestly ordination the bishop lays his hands on the candidate and prays the consecratory prayer; the new priest is vested in the priestly vestments and receives the instruments of his ministry. Many in Kerala still use the old title Achan (father) for priests, a reminder that the priest is to be a father to his people.
Praying for vocations and for our priests

“The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest” (Matthew 9:37–38). Every family can pray for vocations and encourage a son who feels the call.

Pray for your priests and bishops every day. Respect them, help them, and correct with charity when needed. A priest is a man taken from among the people for the people (Hebrews 5:1); he needs the prayer and friendship of his community.
notes: Only a bishop can validly ordain (CCC 1576). Ordination of a bishop requires a mandate from the Pope (in the Latin Church) or the canonical provision of the Eastern Church concerned, in communion with the Pope.
Candidates are formed for many years in seminaries and must be freely chosen, mature, and of sound faith and morals; the Church examines their suitability with care.
Questions about celibacy and married clergy are governed by the law of each Church sui iuris; in the Latin Church priests are bound to celibacy (c. 277).
A priest who leaves the ministry remains a priest by the character received; he may be dispensed from the obligations of the clerical state only by the Holy See.
refs: Lumen Gentium 18–29; Presbyterorum Ordinis; Optatam Totius
Code of Canon Law cc. 1008–1054; Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches cc. 743–775

sub: Ramsha, Lelya and Sapra: how the Syro-Malabar Church sanctifies the day
sec: Praying without ceasing

“Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5:17). From the beginning the Church prayed at fixed hours, as Israel did: “Seven times a day I praise you” (Psalm 119:164). Peter went up to pray at noon, Peter and John went to the temple at the ninth hour (Acts 10:9; 3:1).

The Prayer of the Hours sanctifies the whole day and night: it extends to every hour the praise and thanksgiving of the Eucharist (CCC 1174–1178). It is the prayer of Christ with his Body, the Church, to the Father.
What it is made of

The heart of the Hours is the Psalms, the prayer book of Israel and of Jesus himself. Around them are hymns, readings from Scripture and the Fathers, intercessions and prayers. Each hour has its own character: morning praise for the light of the risen Christ, evening thanksgiving and repentance at the close of the day, night watching for the Lord who comes.
It is not only for priests and religious. Families, prayer groups and parishes can pray at least the morning or evening hour together.
The Hours in our Church

The East Syriac Church counts the day from evening. Its principal hours are Ramsha (evening prayer), Lelya (night prayer, with the Qala d'Shahra, the vigil) and Sapra (morning prayer); monastic communities also keep the daytime hours. The Syro-Malabar Church has published the Hours in Malayalam for use by priests, religious and the faithful.

Ramsha begins with the lighting of the lamp and the incense, and with the psalm of the evening sacrifice (Psalm 141): “Let my prayer be counted as incense before you, and the lifting up of my hands as an evening sacrifice.” Sapra greets the morning with the praise of creation and of Christ, the Light.
How to begin

Begin small: one psalm in the morning and one in the evening; the Our Father three times a day; the Angelus at noon. Learn the evening prayer of your Church and pray it at home with the family; it is the oldest family prayer of Kerala Christians, the sandhyaprarthana at the lighting of the lamp.
Priests, deacons and religious pray the Hours daily on behalf of the whole Church; when you pray with them, your small prayer joins the great prayer of the Church.
notes: Priests and transitional deacons are bound to pray the Liturgy of the Hours daily according to the books of their own Church; permanent deacons as determined by the bishops (c. 276 §2, 3°; CCEO c. 377).
The Prayer of the Hours is the public prayer of the Church; private devotions are good, but they should lead to the liturgy and never replace it (Sacrosanctum Concilium 13).
refs: Syro-Malabar Church, Liturgy of the Hours (Yamaprarthanakal)

sub: Holy water, the cross, blessings and popular piety in the Syro-Malabar tradition
sec: What sacramentals are

Sacramentals are sacred signs instituted by the Church, which resemble the sacraments: they signify spiritual effects obtained through the prayer of the Church. They dispose us to receive the grace of the sacraments and sanctify the various circumstances of life (CCC 1667–1670).

Among them, blessings come first: blessings of persons, of homes and work, of meals, of objects used in prayer. Others are holy water, blessed candles, the crucifix and the cross, medals, the rosary, the scapular, and the consecration of churches and altars.
Not magic, but faith

A sacramental does not work by itself like a charm. Its power comes from the prayer of the Church and from the faith and love with which it is used (CCC 1670). Holy water on the forehead recalls our Baptism; a blessed cross in the home declares that Christ is its Lord; the rosary leads us to meditate on the mysteries of Christ with Mary.

Superstition gives to signs a power they do not have; it is a sin against the first commandment (CCC 2111). Fortune-telling, horoscopes, charms against the evil eye and the like are contrary to faith and must be avoided (CCC 2116–2117).
Popular piety

The faith of our people is expressed in many devotions: processions, novenas, pilgrimages, the lighting of lamps and candles, the veneration of relics and images, the Way of the Cross. The Church values this popular piety and guides it so that it leads to Christ and to the liturgy (CCC 1674–1676).
Vows and offerings (nercha) at shrines are good when they come from faith and gratitude, never when they become a bargain with God or a substitute for conversion.
In our tradition

The St Thomas Christians have always honoured the Cross: the Mar Thoma Sliba in churches, the cross on the gable of homes, the sign of the cross made slowly and fully. Many families keep a prayer corner (with a cross, a lamp and the Bible) where the evening prayer is said.

Traditional blessings include the blessing of a new house (with the priest sprinkling holy water and placing a cross), the blessing of the first rice and of the harvest, and the blessing of children by parents and grandparents. On Denha, water is solemnly blessed in many parishes and taken home.
Blessings in daily life

Ask the priest to bless your home, your new vehicle, your place of work. Parents can bless their children every night with the sign of the cross on the forehead; it is a priestly gesture of the baptised. Keep holy water at home and use it with a prayer.
Before and after meals, at the beginning of a journey, in times of sickness or fear, a short blessing turns ordinary life into prayer.
notes: Blessed objects should be treated with reverence; when worn out, they are burned or buried, not thrown away with rubbish.

Exorcism in the strict sense may be performed only by a priest with the express permission of the bishop (CCC 1673; c. 1172). Those troubled should first be seen by a priest and, where needed, by a doctor; many troubles have natural causes.
Do not buy or sell blessed objects for their blessing; the price is only for the material.
refs: Directory on Popular Piety and the Liturgy (2001)

sub: How the Syro-Malabar Church accompanies the dead and comforts the living
sec: Christian hope before death

“I am the resurrection and the life. Those who believe in me, even though they die, will live” (John 11:25). For Christians death is not the end but a passage: “life is changed, not ended”, as the ancient prayer of the Church says (CCC 1012). The body that was the temple of the Holy Spirit will rise again on the last day.
Therefore the Church accompanies her children to the end with prayer, honours their bodies with reverence, and continues to pray for them after death (CCC 1680–1684).
Praying for the dead

Scripture already praises prayer for the dead, that they might be delivered from their sin (2 Maccabees 12:43–46) (p). Those who die in God's grace but not yet fully purified undergo purification after death, which the Church calls purgatory (CCC 1030–1032).
Our prayers, especially the Eucharistic sacrifice offered for them, almsgiving and works of penance, help the departed. The communion of saints unites the living and the dead in one family of God.
The funeral in our Church

The Syro-Malabar funeral rite unfolds in stations: prayers at the home of the deceased, the procession to the church, the funeral service and Holy Qurbana in the church, and the burial at the cemetery, where the body is laid facing east, awaiting the Lord who will come from the east. The rite is rich in East Syriac hymns of hope in the resurrection.

After the funeral, the family traditionally keeps days of remembrance with Holy Qurbana and prayer, on days fixed by local custom, such as the seventh day, the thirtieth or forty-first day, and the anniversary (Ormma). The Friday before the Great Fast is the commemoration of all the faithful departed, and November is dedicated to praying for them.
Grief and consolation

Jesus wept at the tomb of his friend Lazarus (John 11:35). Christian faith does not forbid tears; it gives them hope. Families should be allowed to grieve, and the parish community should surround them with prayer, presence and practical help.
Visit the bereaved after the funeral, not only on the day. Remember the dead by name at family prayer and on anniversaries. Teach children that we will see our loved ones again in Christ.
notes: The Church earnestly recommends burial of the body; cremation is permitted when it is not chosen for reasons contrary to Christian faith. The ashes must be kept in a sacred place (cemetery or church), not scattered, divided or kept at home (Ad resurgendum cum Christo, 2016; c. 1176 §3).

Funeral rites are not denied to Catholics except in the cases foreseen by law; when in doubt, the bishop decides (c. 1184). Pastors should show special compassion to families in tragic deaths, including suicide, for which the Church prays and hopes in God's mercy (CCC 2283).
Lavish display at funerals and feasts that burden the family are contrary to Christian simplicity; offer Masses and alms for the departed instead.
refs: Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith, Ad resurgendum cum Christo (2016)
